quotes.t: Do not repeat the tactics which have gained you one victory, but let your methods be regulated by the infinite variety of circumstances.
Therefore the clever combatant imposes his will on the enemy, but does not allow the enemy's will to be imposed on him.
If the enemy is taking his ease, he can harass him; if well supplied with food, he can starve him out; if quietly encamped, he can force him to move.
To think you can make a man richer by putting on a tax is like a man thinking that he can stand in a bucket and lift himself up by the handle.
quotes.source: Speech in the House of Commons, 28 May 1903

quotes.t: The truth is incontrovertible. Panic may resent it, ignorance may deride it, malice may distort it, but there it is.
quotes.source: Speech in the House of Commons, 17 May 1916

quotes.t: To build may have to be the slow and laborious task of years. To destroy can be the thoughtless act of a single day.
Purity, patience, and perseverance are the three essentials to success, and above all, love.
Never think there is anything impossible for the soul. It is the greatest heresy to think so. If there is sin, this is the only sin — to say that you are weak, or others are weak.
quotes.source: Vivekananda: His Call to the Nation

quotes.t: It is the calm, forgiving, equable, well-balanced mind that does the greatest amount of work.
The ache for home lives in all of us, the safe place where we can go as we are and not be questioned.
quotes.source: All God's Children Need Traveling Shoes

quotes.t: Music was my refuge. I could crawl into the space between the notes and curl my back to loneliness.
quotes.source: Singin' and Swingin' and Gettin' Merry Like Christmas

quotes.t: In the flush of love's light, we dare be brave.
Let me define a leader. He must have vision and passion and not be afraid of any problem. Instead, he should know how to defeat it. Most importantly, he must work with integrity.
Confidence and hard work is the best medicine to kill the disease called failure. It will make you a successful person.
The purpose of education is to make good human beings with skill and expertise.
You are where you are in life because of what you believe is possible for yourself.
The whole point of being alive is to evolve into the complete person you were intended to be.
I believe that one of life's greatest risks is never daring to risk.
Justice cannot be for one side alone, but must be for both.
We are afraid to care too much, for fear that the other person does not care at all.
I have spent many years of my life in opposition, and I rather like the role.
You can have no dominion greater or less than that over yourself.
quotes.source: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci

quotes.t: Ask counsel of him who rules himself well.
quotes.source: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci

quotes.t: He who thinks little, errs much.
quotes.source: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci

quotes.t: Man is only truly great when he acts from the passions; never irresistible but when he appeals to the imagination.
There is no index of character so sure as the voice.
I am a Conservative to preserve all that is good in our constitution, a Radical to remove all that is bad.
All men seek happiness. This is without exception. Whatever different means they employ, they all tend to this end.
The knowledge of God is very far from the love of Him.
The last thing one settles in writing a book is what one should put in first.
Only put off until tomorrow what you are willing to die having left undone.
When art critics get together they talk about form and structure and meaning. When artists get together they talk about where you can buy cheap turpentine.
We don't grow older, we grow riper.
He who has a why to live for can bear almost any how.
The great epochs of our life are the occasions when we gain the courage to rebaptize our evil qualities as our best qualities.
You must be ready to burn yourself in your own flame; how could you rise anew if you have not first become ashes?
I have walked that long road to freedom. I have tried not to falter; I have made missteps along the way.
It is in your hands, to make a better world for all who live in it.
There is no easy walk to freedom anywhere, and many of us will have to pass through the valley of the shadow of death again and again before we reach the mountaintop of our desires.
Joy is prayer; joy is strength; joy is love; joy is a net of love by which you can catch souls.
The miracle is not that we do this work, but that we are happy to do it.
We do not need guns and bombs to bring peace, we need love and compassion.
Conscience is God present in man.
There are no weeds, and no worthless men. There are only bad farmers.
You who suffer because you love, love still more. To die of love is to live by it.
Seeking what is true is not seeking what is desirable.
I rebel; therefore I exist.
Nothing is more despicable than respect based on fear.
You don't need anybody to tell you who you are or what you are. You are what you are!
I believe in everything until it's disproved. So I believe in fairies, the myths, dragons. It all exists, even if it's in your mind.
We live in a world where we have to hide to make love, while violence is practiced in broad daylight.
We are made wise not by the recollection of our past, but by the responsibility for our future.
If you cannot get rid of the family skeleton, you may as well make it dance.
Success does not consist in never making mistakes but in never making the same one a second time.
Wisdom is by far the greatest part of joy.
Look and you will find it - what is unsought will go undetected.
Foolishness is indeed the sister of wickedness.
The tragedy of life is what dies inside a man while he lives.
There are two means of refuge from the misery of life - music and cats.
Do something for somebody every day for which you do not get paid.
From the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step.
quotes.source: Remark on the retreat from Russia, 1812 (recorded by Abbé du Pradt)

quotes.t: When we resist change, it's called suffering.
quotes.source: Living Beautifully with Uncertainty and Change

quotes.t: The whole moon and the entire sky are reflected in dewdrops on the grass, or even in one drop of water.
It is not enough to be industrious; so are the ants. What are you industrious about?
quotes.source: Letter to H. G. O. Blake, 16 November 1857

quotes.t: One generation plants the trees, another gets the shade.
That future is not one of ease or resting but of incessant striving so that we may fulfil the pledges we have so often taken and the one we shall take today.
But the chief penalty is to be governed by someone worse if a man will not himself hold office and rule.
Whichever you do, you will repent it.
If God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him.
quotes.source: Épître à l'auteur du livre des Trois Imposteurs (1769)

quotes.t: No space of regret can make amends for one life's opportunities misused.
If I read a book and it makes my whole body so cold no fire can ever warm me, I know that is poetry.
He that falls in love with himself will have no rivals.
Nothing in all the world is more dangerous than sincere ignorance and conscientious stupidity.
One half of the world cannot understand the pleasures of the other.
Wrong does not cease to be wrong because the majority share in it.
quotes.source: The Law of Violence and the Law of Love

quotes.t: I postpone death by living, by suffering, by error, by risking, by giving, by losing.
The best remedy for those who are afraid, lonely or unhappy is to go outside, somewhere where they can be quiet, alone with the heavens, nature and God.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl (23 February 1944)

quotes.t: It takes something more than intelligence to act intelligently.
There is only one way to eat an elephant: a bite at a time.
From the errors of others, a wise man corrects his own.
The first duty of man is to conquer fear; he must get rid of it, he cannot act till then.
quotes.source: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History

quotes.t: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.
Invention, it must be humbly admitted, does not consist in creating out of void, but out of chaos.
I almost wish we were butterflies and liv'd but three summer days — three such days with you I could fill with more delight than fifty common years could ever contain.
Positively, my social philosophy may be said to be enshrined in three words: liberty, equality and fraternity.
Not to know what happened before you were born is to be a child forever.
Reading furnishes the mind only with materials of knowledge; it is thinking that makes what we read ours.
quotes.source: Of the Conduct of the Understanding

quotes.t: My love is like a red, red rose that's newly sprung in June.
Facts are stubborn things; and whatever may be our wishes, our inclinations, or the dictates of our passion, they cannot alter the state of facts and evidence.
quotes.source: Argument in the Boston Massacre trial, 1770

quotes.t: Men, their rights, and nothing more; women, their rights, and nothing less.
All that we see or seem is but a dream within a dream.
Poetry is at bottom a criticism of life.
He who has done his best for his own time has lived for all times.
From a little spark may burst a flame.
Long is the way and hard, that out of hell leads up to light.
Earth's crammed with heaven, and every common bush afire with God.
If the fool would persist in his folly he would become wise.
quotes.source: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell

quotes.t: Nature, to be commanded, must be obeyed.
A little learning is a dangerous thing.
No man chooses evil because it is evil; he only mistakes it for happiness, the good he seeks.
quotes.source: A Vindication of the Rights of Men

A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.bio: Indian aerospace scientist and the 11th President of India (2002-2007), known as the 'Missile Man of India'.

Albert Camus.bio: French-Algerian writer and philosopher, author of The Stranger; Nobel Prize in Literature 1957.

Albert Schweitzer.bio: Albert Schweitzer was an Alsatian theologian, musician and physician who founded a hospital at Lambaréné in Gabon and served there for decades. His philosophy of reverence for life and his Bach scholarship earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952.

Alexander Pope.bio: English poet and master of the heroic couplet. His works include An Essay on Criticism, The Rape of the Lock and An Essay on Man, along with celebrated translations of Homer.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

B.R. Ambedkar.bio: Indian jurist and social reformer who chaired the drafting of India's Constitution and campaigned against caste discrimination.

Benjamin Disraeli.bio: British statesman who served twice as Prime Minister and led the Conservative Party. He was also a successful novelist, writing books such as Coningsby and Sybil.
Benjamin Disraeli.credit: Cornelius Jabez Hughes, Public domain (File: File:Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield.jpg)

Benjamin Franklin.bio: American polymath - printer, scientist, diplomat - and a Founding Father of the United States.

Blaise Pascal.bio: French mathematician, physicist and philosopher, author of the Pensées.
Blaise Pascal.credit: unknown; a copy of the painting of François II Quesnel, which was made for Gérard Edelinck en 1691, Public domain

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

Cicero.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, lawyer and orator considered the master of Latin prose. His speeches, letters and philosophical works, including On Friendship, transmitted Greek philosophy to the Roman world.

Dante Alighieri.bio: Italian poet, author of the Divine Comedy, a cornerstone of world literature.

Desmond Tutu.bio: South African Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1984) who campaigned against apartheid.

Dogen.bio: Founder of the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shōbōgenzō, a landmark of Buddhist philosophy.

Edgar Allan Poe.bio: Edgar Allan Poe was an American writer and poet known for tales of mystery and the macabre such as "The Raven" and "The Fall of the House of Usher". He is credited with inventing the detective-fiction genre.

Eleanor Roosevelt.bio: Eleanor Roosevelt was the longest-serving First Lady of the United States, from 1933 to 1945, and reinvented the role as a platform for civil rights and social reform. Afterward she became a US delegate to the United Nations and chaired the commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
Eleanor Roosevelt.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain (File: Eleanor Roosevelt portrait 1933.jpg)

Elizabeth Barrett Browning.bio: English poet best known for Sonnets from the Portuguese, including Sonnet 43.

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Francis Bacon.bio: Francis Bacon was an English philosopher, statesman and essayist who championed the empirical method of inquiry. His Essays and his plan for the reform of learning in the Novum Organum helped lay the groundwork of modern science.

Friedrich Nietzsche.bio: German philosopher known for Thus Spoke Zarathustra and the concept of the will to power.

Friedrich Schiller.bio: German poet, philosopher, historian and playwright; author of the Wallenstein trilogy, Don Carlos and the 'Ode to Joy'.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.bio: Russian novelist, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

George Bernard Shaw.bio: Irish playwright and critic; author of Pygmalion; Nobel Prize in Literature 1925.
George Bernard Shaw.credit: Sussman, Public domain (File: George Bernard Shaw, playwright (SAYRE 9001).jpg)

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jawaharlal Nehru.bio: Leader of India's independence movement and the country's first Prime Minister (1947-1964).

John Adams.bio: John Adams was an American statesman and Founding Father who served as the first vice president and second president of the United States (1797–1801). A leader of the independence movement, he died on 4 July 1826, the same day as Thomas Jefferson.

John Keats.bio: English Romantic poet of the great Odes, including Ode to a Nightingale.

John Lennon.bio: English singer-songwriter, co-founder of the Beatles and solo artist known for Imagine.

John Locke.bio: John Locke was an English philosopher and physician whose ideas on empiricism, natural rights and government by consent shaped the Enlightenment and modern liberal thought. His major works include 'An Essay Concerning Human Understanding' (1689) and 'Two Treatises of Government' (1689).

John Milton.bio: English poet best known for the epic poem Paradise Lost (1667).

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Leonardo da Vinci.bio: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian Renaissance painter, engineer and anatomist whose notebooks reveal an insatiable curiosity about nature and art. He painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and filled thousands of pages with studies, inventions and observations.
Leonardo da Vinci.credit: Leonardo da Vinci, Public domain (File: Leonardo self.jpg)

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Mary Shelley.bio: English novelist, author of Frankenstein, a founding work of science fiction.

Mary Wollstonecraft.bio: Mary Wollstonecraft was an English writer and advocate of women's rights, best known for A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792). She argued that women are not naturally inferior to men but appear so because of a lack of education. She was the mother of Frankenstein author Mary Shelley.

Matthew Arnold.bio: English poet and cultural critic; author of 'Dover Beach' and Culture and Anarchy.

Maya Angelou.bio: American poet and memoirist best known for I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969).
Maya Angelou.credit: Bee Photos by Ryan Marty, Public domain

Mother Teresa.bio: Albanian-Indian Catholic nun who founded the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata; Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1979).
Mother Teresa.credit: John Mathew Smith & www.celebrity-photos.com from Laurel  Maryland, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0

Napoleon Bonaparte.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French in 1804. His Napoleonic Wars reshaped Europe, and his Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems worldwide. He died in exile on Saint Helena.

Nelson Mandela.role: Anti-apartheid leader, President of South Africa
Nelson Mandela.bio: South African anti-apartheid revolutionary who spent 27 years in prison and became the country's first Black president in 1994.

Oprah Winfrey.bio: American talk-show host and media executive whose long-running show made her one of the most influential broadcasters in history.
Oprah Winfrey.credit: US Embassy South Africa, Public domain

Pablo Picasso.bio: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist who co-founded Cubism and reinvented his style across a career of nearly eighty years. Works such as Les Demoiselles d'Avignon and Guernica made him the most famous and influential artist of the 20th century.
Pablo Picasso.credit: Didier Descouens, Public domain (File: File:(Barcelona) Retrat de Picasso - Pablo Gargallo - Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya.jpg)

Pema Chodron.bio: Pema Chodron is an American nun in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and a widely read author and teacher. Her books, including When Things Fall Apart, bring Buddhist teachings on compassion and difficulty to a broad audience.

Plato.bio: Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and author of The Republic.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Robert Burns.bio: Scottish poet and lyricist, author of Auld Lang Syne.
Robert Burns.credit: John Beugo after Alexander Nasmyth, Public domain

Socrates.bio: Greek philosopher of Athens, central figure of Western philosophy; left no writings.

Sophocles.bio: Sophocles was an Athenian tragedian who wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. Oedipus Rex and Antigone, his most famous works, set the pattern for Western tragedy.

Sun Tzu.bio: Ancient Chinese general traditionally credited with The Art of War, a treatise on strategy studied worldwide for over two thousand years.
Sun Tzu.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: 吴司马孙武.jpg)

Susan B. Anthony.bio: Susan B. Anthony spent more than fifty years campaigning for women's right to vote, co-founding the National Woman Suffrage Association with Elizabeth Cady Stanton. Arrested for voting in 1872, she died fourteen years before the Nineteenth Amendment finally secured women's suffrage.

Swami Vivekananda.bio: Indian Hindu monk who introduced Vedanta and Yoga to the West; famous for his 1893 Chicago Parliament of Religions address.
Swami Vivekananda.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: Swami Vivekananda at Parliament of Religions.jpg)

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Victor Hugo.bio: French poet and novelist, author of Les Misérables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame.
Victor Hugo.credit: Étienne Carjat, Public domain (File: Victor Hugo by Étienne Carjat 1876 - full.jpg)

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

William Blake.bio: William Blake was an English poet, painter and printmaker whose illuminated books, including Songs of Innocence and of Experience and The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, were largely unrecognised in his lifetime. He is now considered a seminal figure of Romantic poetry and visual art.

Winston Churchill.bio: British prime minister during the Second World War and Nobel laureate in Literature.
